question: A measurement is described either by a family of orthogonal projectors P_j (positive, summing to the identity, and mutually orthogonal P_jP_k = 0 for j != k) or, more generally, by a family of positive operators E_k that are positive and sum to the identity but are not required to be orthogonal or idempotent. For a system in state rho, in both cases outcome label k occurs with probability tr(rho E_k) (respectively tr(rho P_j)). Explain precisely why the projector family determines a well-defined post-measurement state for each outcome, whereas the general positive-operator family does not; identify exactly which of the three projector properties is responsible for the probabilities being a valid distribution and which is responsible for a canonical state update, and state what extra structure is needed to assign an update rule to the general family.
reference_answer: Validity of the probabilities needs only positivity and completeness: each tr(rho E_k) >= 0 because rho and E_k are both positive, and sum_k tr(rho E_k) = tr(rho (sum_k E_k)) = tr(rho) = 1 by completeness and the trace being linear with tr(rho)=1. Orthogonality is not used here. The canonical post-measurement state, on the other hand, relies on idempotency/orthogonality: for a projective measurement the updated state after outcome j is (P_j rho P_j)/tr(rho P_j), and orthogonality P_jP_k = delta_{jk}P_j is exactly what makes repeated or compatible measurements consistent and makes P_j a genuine projection onto an eigenspace. A general positive family {E_k} has no distinguished square root, so there is no unique way to collapse the state: any operators M_k with M_k^dagger M_k = E_k give a legitimate update rho -> (M_k rho M_k^dagger)/tr(rho E_k), and different choices of M_k (differing by a left unitary, M_k -> V_k M_k) yield different post-measurement states while leaving every probability tr(rho E_k) unchanged. Hence the general family fixes only the outcome statistics, not the state update; to recover a definite update one must supply the measurement operators M_k (equivalently, realize the family as a projective measurement on a larger system together with an environment, after which a projective update on the enlarged space is well defined).

rubric.criterion: States that positivity + completeness alone make tr(rho E_k) a probability distribution, with the explicit sum_k tr(rho E_k) = tr(rho) = 1, and that orthogonality is not needed for this
Gives the projective update (P_j rho P_j)/tr(rho P_j) and ties its canonical status to idempotency/orthogonality

Explains that a general positive family has no unique square root, so updates M_k rho M_k^dagger / tr(rho E_k) with M_k^dagger M_k = E_k are non-unique (M_k -> V_k M_k) yet leave all probabilities fixed
Concludes the general family determines only statistics, and names the extra data (measurement operators / a larger-system realization) needed to fix an update

semantic_steps.claim: Positivity and completeness give tr(rho E_k) >= 0 and sum_k tr(rho E_k) = tr(rho) = 1, a valid distribution.
Projector idempotency/orthogonality yields the canonical update (P_j rho P_j)/tr(rho P_j).
A general positive family lacks a unique square root, so M_k -> V_k M_k changes the update but not tr(rho E_k).

question: On a two-part system the partial transpose acts by transposing only the second factor of each elementary tensor while leaving the first factor fixed, extended linearly. Call a joint state separable if it is a probabilistic mixture of product states. (a) Prove that every separable state stays positive under the partial transpose, so that a single negative eigenvalue of the partial transpose certifies entanglement. (b) Illustrate on the two-qubit maximally entangled state whose density matrix has 1/2 on the four corners of the 4x4 matrix and 0 elsewhere: compute its partial transpose and exhibit the negative eigenvalue. (c) State precisely the converse boundary - for which local dimensions is a positive partial transpose also sufficient for separability, and what is the name and significance of the states that violate the converse in larger dimensions.
reference_answer: (a) Write a separable state as a mixture sum_i p_i (omega_i tensor sigma_i) with p_i >= 0 and omega_i, sigma_i positive states. The partial transpose is linear and transposes only the second factor, so it sends this to sum_i p_i (omega_i tensor sigma_i^T). Transposition preserves positivity (X and X^T have the same eigenvalues), hence each sigma_i^T is positive, each tensor factor is positive, and a nonnegative combination of positive operators is positive. Therefore the partial transpose of any separable state is positive. Contrapositive: if the partial transpose has a negative eigenvalue the state cannot be separable, i.e. it is entangled. (b) The given matrix is (1/2) times the matrix with ones at the four corner positions (1,1),(1,4),(4,1),(4,4). Transposing the second qubit swaps the roles of the off-diagonal corner entries with the (2,3)/(3,2) block; the result is (1/2) times the swap-type matrix with 1 on the diagonal and 1 in the (2,3) and (3,2) entries. Its eigenvalues are +1/2 (multiplicity 3) and -1/2 (the antisymmetric combination), so there is a negative eigenvalue -1/2 and the state is entangled. (c) The positivity of the partial transpose is only necessary in general. It is also sufficient for separability exactly when the product of the two local dimensions is at most 6 (the 2x2 and 2x3 cases). In every higher dimension there exist states that are positive under partial transpose yet entangled; these are called bound entangled states, and their existence shows the criterion cannot detect all entanglement and that distillable entanglement is strictly stronger than mere entanglement.

Draws the contrapositive conclusion that a negative partial-transpose eigenvalue certifies entanglement
Computes the partial transpose of the given corner-supported state and exhibits the eigenvalue -1/2
States the sufficiency boundary (product of local dimensions <= 6) and names bound entangled states as the higher-dimensional counterexamples to the converse

question: A quantum state is defined to be an operator rho that is positive (nonnegative expectation in every vector) and has trace one. Prove directly from this definition that the set of states is convex: given states rho_1, ..., rho_n and probabilities p_1, ..., p_n (nonnegative, summing to one), show that rho = sum_i p_i rho_i is again a state. Identify which hypothesis on the p_i is needed for positivity and which for the trace condition, and give a one-line reason why the boundary of this convex set is exactly the pure states.
reference_answer: Positivity: for any vector phi, <phi| rho |phi> = sum_i p_i <phi| rho_i |phi>. Each <phi| rho_i |phi> >= 0 because rho_i is positive, and each p_i >= 0 (nonnegativity of the weights), so the sum is a nonnegative combination of nonnegative numbers and is >= 0; hence rho >= 0. This step uses only p_i >= 0. Trace: by linearity of the trace, tr(rho) = sum_i p_i tr(rho_i) = sum_i p_i * 1 = sum_i p_i = 1, where the last equality is the normalization sum_i p_i = 1 of the probability weights. So this step uses the weights summing to one. Both defining conditions hold, so rho is a state and the set is convex. The extreme points (boundary that cannot be written as a nontrivial mixture) are precisely the rank-one projectors, i.e. the pure states, since any state of rank >= 2 can be split along its spectral decomposition into a nontrivial convex combination of orthogonal lower-rank states.

rubric.criterion: Proves positivity of the mixture via <phi|rho|phi> = sum_i p_i <phi|rho_i|phi> >= 0 and names p_i >= 0 as the hypothesis used
Proves tr(rho) = sum_i p_i = 1 by linearity of trace and names normalization sum_i p_i = 1 as the hypothesis used
Concludes rho satisfies both defining conditions, so the state set is convex

semantic_steps.claim: The mixture is positive because <phi|rho|phi> is a nonnegative combination of nonnegative terms, using p_i >= 0.
The mixture has unit trace because tr is linear and the weights sum to one.

question: A mixed state can be written as a probabilistic mixture of pure states |psi_i> with weights p_i; such a list is called a realizing ensemble. Prove that a mixed state has more than one realizing ensemble by the following explicit construction. Set unnormalized vectors |psi'_i> = sqrt(p_i) |psi_i>, so that the state equals sum_i |psi'_i><psi'_i|. Let V be any rectangular matrix with k >= r rows and r columns whose columns are orthonormal (so V with its conjugate transpose on the left gives the r-by-r identity). Define |phi'_j> = sum_l V_{jl} |psi'_l> for j = 1, ..., k. Show that the k outer products |phi'_j><phi'_j| again sum to the same state, and hence (after renormalizing) give a generally different, and generally longer, pure-state ensemble for it. Explain why genuinely new ensembles exist.
reference_answer: Compute sum_{j=1}^k |phi'_j><phi'_j| = sum_j (sum_l V_{jl} |psi'_l>)(sum_m V_{jm}^* <psi'_m|) = sum_{l,m} (sum_j V_{jm}^* V_{jl}) |psi'_l><psi'_m|. The inner sum over j is the (m,l) entry of the matrix product (V-conjugate-transpose) V, which equals delta_{ml} because the columns of V are orthonormal (V^dagger V = I_r). Hence the double sum collapses to sum_l |psi'_l><psi'_l| = rho, the original state. Writing q_j = <phi'_j|phi'_j> and |phi_j> = q_j^{-1/2} |phi'_j> (for q_j > 0) gives rho = sum_j q_j |phi_j><phi_j|, a bona fide pure-state ensemble with k terms. Because V only has to be an isometry (orthonormal columns), there are infinitely many admissible choices: any k >= r and any r-column isometry works, and distinct isometries produce distinct, generally non-proportional vectors |phi_j>, so the ensemble is genuinely new. In particular one can take k strictly larger than r, giving an ensemble with more pure components than the spectral (eigenvalue) ensemble; this shows a mixed state has infinitely many realizing ensembles and that the decomposition into pure states is far from unique.

Uses the orthonormal-columns hypothesis V^dagger V = I to get delta_{ml}, collapsing the sum back to rho
Renormalizes to q_j, |phi_j> to produce a valid k-term pure-state ensemble equal to the same state
Explains that the freedom in choosing the isometry V (any k >= r) yields infinitely many, generally distinct ensembles

question: Call a bipartite state a product state if it factorizes as a single tensor product of local states, and separable if it is a probabilistic mixture of product states. (a) Show that in a product state the outcomes of any two local measurements are statistically independent (the joint expectation factorizes). (b) Exhibit a concrete separable two-qubit state that is NOT a product state and compute a pair of local measurements whose outcomes are correlated, demonstrating that separable states can carry classical correlation even though each term in the mixture is uncorrelated. (c) Reconcile this with the textbook remark that a PURE separable state is automatically a product state - i.e. explain why your correlated example must be mixed.
reference_answer: (a) For a product state omega tensor sigma and local measurement effects E on the first system and F on the second, the joint probability is tr[(omega tensor sigma)(E tensor F)] = tr(omega E) tr(sigma F), the product of the two marginal probabilities. Hence the two outcomes are independent and uncorrelated. (b) Take the classically correlated state rho = (1/2)(|0><0| tensor |0><0|) + (1/2)(|1><1| tensor |1><1|). It is separable (an equal mixture of the two product states |00><00| and |11><11|) but it is not a single product omega tensor sigma: its marginals are both the maximally mixed (1/2)I, whose product (1/4)I is full rank, while rho has rank 2, so rho != marginal tensor marginal. Measuring the first qubit in the computational basis (outcome a in {0,1}) and the second likewise (outcome b) gives joint probabilities Pr(0,0)=Pr(1,1)=1/2, Pr(0,1)=Pr(1,0)=0. The outcomes are perfectly correlated (a = b always) even though Pr(a=0)=Pr(b=0)=1/2, so Pr(a,b) != Pr(a)Pr(b); the correlation is exactly the shared classical index of the mixture. (c) A pure separable state is by definition an extreme point that is also a mixture of products; being extreme, the mixture must be trivial, so it equals one product term omega tensor sigma, and by part (a) it is uncorrelated. Therefore any separable state exhibiting correlation must be a nontrivial mixture, i.e. mixed - consistent with the example, whose rank is 2 and which is a genuine average over two distinct product states.

Explains that a pure separable state is extreme hence a single product (uncorrelated), so a correlated separable state must be mixed

question: The trace norm of an operator X is the sum of its singular values. Prove the variational characterization that this norm equals the maximum, over all unitaries U, of the absolute value of the trace of (X times U). Use a singular value decomposition X = W Sigma V-dagger (with W, V unitary and Sigma the diagonal matrix of singular values) and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product <A,B> = tr(A-dagger B). Then exhibit a specific unitary U that attains the maximum, and explain why this shows the trace norm cannot be reproduced by testing against any fixed single unitary.
reference_answer: Upper bound: for any unitary U, |tr(X U)| = |tr(W Sigma V-dagger U)| = |tr(Sigma V-dagger U W)|. Put Y = V-dagger U W, which is unitary, so its diagonal entries Y_{ii} satisfy |Y_{ii}| <= 1 (a unit vector's component). Then |tr(Sigma Y)| = |sum_i s_i Y_{ii}| <= sum_i s_i |Y_{ii}| <= sum_i s_i = ||X||_1, using s_i >= 0. (Equivalently, by Cauchy-Schwarz on <X-dagger, U> = tr(X U) one bounds the overlap by the product of the trace norm and the operator norm 1 of U.) So |tr(X U)| <= ||X||_1 for every unitary U, hence the max is at most ||X||_1. Attainment: choose U = V W-dagger. Then X U = W Sigma V-dagger V W-dagger = W Sigma W-dagger, so tr(X U) = tr(Sigma) = sum_i s_i = ||X||_1, which is real and nonnegative; thus the bound is achieved and the maximum equals ||X||_1. Finally, the optimal U = V W-dagger depends on the singular vectors of X, i.e. on X itself; a fixed unitary chosen in advance will generally fail to align with Sigma and give |tr(X U)| strictly below ||X||_1, so no single fixed unitary computes the trace norm for all X - the maximization over U is essential.

Explains the optimal U depends on X's singular vectors, so no fixed single unitary reproduces the norm; the maximization is needed

question: A two-qubit state invariant under all local transformations of the form U tensor U can be written with a single real parameter x in [-1,1] as rho(x) = ((2 - x)/6) I + ((2x - 1)/6) F, where I is the identity and F is the swap operator (F|a>|b> = |b>|a>). It is given that x equals the trace overlap tr(F rho). Determine the exact threshold in x at which rho(x) becomes entangled, prove the entangled direction using the partial-transpose test (you may use that the partial transpose of F is twice the projector onto the maximally entangled state, and that the identity resolves into the four Bell projectors), and explain in one or two sentences why the separable direction holds without appealing to any low-dimension sufficiency shortcut.
reference_answer: Threshold: rho(x) is entangled if and only if x < 0; equivalently it is separable exactly for x in [0,1]. Entangled direction (x < 0): take the partial transpose of rho(x). Using (F)^{T_B} = 2 P_+, where P_+ is the projector onto the maximally entangled state, and I^{T_B} = I, linearity gives rho(x)^{T_B} = ((2 - x)/6) I + ((2x - 1)/3) P_+. Expanding I = P_+ + P_- + P_{psi+} + P_{psi-} in the Bell basis, the operator is diagonal in that basis with eigenvalue y = (2 - x)/6 on the three Bell states orthogonal to P_+, and eigenvalue z = (2 - x)/6 + (2x - 1)/3 on P_+. Simplifying, z = (2 - x)/6 + (4x - 2)/6 = (3x)/6 = x/2. Hence z = x/2 < 0 precisely when x < 0, giving a negative partial-transpose eigenvalue and so entanglement for all x in [-1,0). Separable direction (x >= 0): for any product state omega tensor sigma the swap overlap tr[(omega tensor sigma) F] = tr(omega sigma) >= 0 because both are positive operators (the swap trick), and this extends by linearity to every mixture of products; so every separable state has tr(F rho) = x >= 0. Conversely any x in [0,1] is realized by averaging (twirling) a suitable product state, which stays a mixture of products and hence separable. This argument is valid in any local dimension, so it does not rely on the special low-dimension sufficiency of the partial-transpose test.

Concludes the negative eigenvalue z = x/2 < 0 for x < 0 proves entanglement via the partial-transpose test
Proves the separable direction via the swap-overlap positivity tr(omega sigma) >= 0 extended to mixtures, noting dimension-independence

semantic_steps.claim: In the Bell basis the P_+ eigenvalue is z = (2-x)/6 + (2x-1)/3 = x/2, negative iff x < 0, so entangled for x < 0.
For x >= 0 separability follows from tr(F omega tensor sigma) = tr(omega sigma) >= 0 extended to mixtures, independent of dimension.

question: Suppose a non-unitary matrix A acting on n qubits is embedded as the top-left block of a larger unitary, in the sense that applying the unitary to an input with the ancilla register prepared in all-zeros, and then measuring the ancillas and keeping only the all-zeros outcome, applies A to the system state. More generally the embedded block equals A divided by a positive subnormalization factor alpha. For an input system state |b>, derive the probability of the kept (all-zeros) outcome, express it in terms of A, |b> and alpha, and explain two consequences: how the norm of A|b> can be recovered from the measured success probability, and why choosing alpha too large is harmful. Confirm the output state conditioned on success is the correctly normalized version of A|b>.
reference_answer: Apply the unitary to |0...0>|b>. By the block structure the component in the all-zeros ancilla sector is |0...0> (A/alpha)|b>, and the rest is orthogonal to the all-zeros ancilla subspace. The probability of measuring the ancillas in all-zeros is the squared norm of that component: p(0) = ||(A/alpha)|b>||^2 = (1/alpha^2) <b| A-dagger A |b> = ||A|b>||^2 / alpha^2. In the exact one-ancilla case alpha = 1 this is simply p(0) = ||A|b>||^2 = <b|A-dagger A|b>. Consequence 1 (norm recovery): the norm that is 'lost' when the output is renormalized is encoded in the success probability, since ||A|b>|| = alpha sqrt(p(0)); measuring p(0) (by repetition) therefore recovers ||A|b>||. Consequence 2 (cost of large alpha): p(0) scales as 1/alpha^2, so an unnecessarily large alpha makes the all-zeros outcome exponentially unlikely and the scheme requires on the order of alpha^2/||A|b>||^2 repetitions (or amplitude amplification) to succeed, which is why one wants the smallest valid alpha (at least the operator norm of A). Output state on success: dividing the kept component by its own norm gives (A/alpha)|b> / ||(A/alpha)|b>|| = A|b> / ||A|b>||, the correctly normalized image of |b> under A, independent of alpha and of the irrelevant orthogonal part of the unitary.

rubric.criterion: Derives p(0) = ||(A/alpha)|b>||^2 = ||A|b>||^2/alpha^2 = (1/alpha^2)<b|A-dagger A|b> by taking the squared norm of the all-zeros-ancilla component
States the exact-case p(0) = ||A|b>||^2 and that the output on success is A|b>/||A|b>||, independent of alpha
Explains norm recovery ||A|b>|| = alpha sqrt(p(0)) from the measured success probability
Explains that p(0) ~ 1/alpha^2 makes large alpha harmful (vanishing success probability / many repetitions)

p(0) = ||A|b>||^2/alpha^2 = (1/alpha^2)<b|A-dagger A|b>, so ||A|b>|| = alpha sqrt(p(0)).

question: When a matrix A is embedded (up to a positive factor alpha) as the all-zeros block of a larger unitary, so that A/alpha is a submatrix of a unitary, prove the necessary scaling constraint on alpha. First prove the auxiliary fact that any submatrix block of a unitary has operator norm at most 1. Deduce the sharp lower bound alpha must satisfy in terms of the operator norm of A, explain why an exact unit-factor embedding is impossible when A has operator norm bigger than 1, and state what role alpha then plays and whether the bound alone guarantees an efficiently implementable embedding.
reference_answer: Submatrix-norm fact: let U be unitary and let B = P U Q be a block, where P and Q are projectors onto the output and input index sets of the block (equivalently B = <0^m| U |0^m> as an operator on the system register). For any unit input vector v (extended by zeros outside the block), ||B v|| = ||P U (Q v)|| <= ||U (Q v)|| = ||Q v|| <= ||v|| = 1, since projectors are norm-nonincreasing and U is norm-preserving. Taking the supremum over unit v gives ||B|| <= 1. Lower bound on alpha: if A/alpha is such a block of a unitary, then ||A/alpha|| <= 1, i.e. ||A|| <= alpha, so alpha >= ||A|| is necessary. In particular if ||A|| > 1 there is no exact embedding with alpha = 1 (a unit-factor block would force ||A|| <= 1); one must take alpha >= ||A|| > 1. Role of alpha: it rescales A so that A/alpha fits inside a unitary as a contraction, at the cost of a success probability that falls like 1/alpha^2; the smallest admissible alpha is the operator norm ||A|| (achieved by a singular-value dilation). Finally, the inequality alpha >= ||A|| is only a necessary existence condition on the scale: it does not by itself provide a circuit, since constructing a unitary whose block is A/alpha and that is implementable with few elementary gates requires further structure or oracle access to A; the bound guarantees feasibility of the scale, not efficiency of implementation.

question: To certify that an (m+n)-qubit unitary U exactly embeds an n-qubit matrix A as its all-zeros block with unit factor, one checks the entrywise identities <0^m, i| U |0^m, j> = A_{ij} for all computational-basis indices i, j. (a) Explain operationally how each such entry can be read off by preparing the ancilla in all-zeros and the system in basis state j, applying U, and overlapping with the all-zeros-ancilla basis state i, and how a composed unitary U = U_B U_C lets one evaluate the two halves independently before overlapping. (b) Explain why checking all entries equal to A_{ij} is equivalent to the exact operator identity (all-zeros block of U equals A), but why for an APPROXIMATE embedding entrywise closeness of each A_{ij} is NOT the right accuracy notion: give the quantity that the definition of approximate embedding actually controls and explain how it can be large even when every entry error is tiny.
reference_answer: (a) Preparing |0^m>|j>, applying U and projecting onto <0^m, i| extracts exactly the number <0^m, i| U |0^m, j>, which by construction is the (i,j) entry of the all-zeros block; running over all i, j reads off the whole block. If U = U_B U_C, then <0^m, i| U_B U_C |0^m, j> = (U_B-dagger |0^m, i>)-dagger (U_C |0^m, j>), so one can prepare and evaluate the two states U_B-dagger|0^m,i> and U_C|0^m,j> independently and take their inner product; this is the standard way to verify a product construction entry by entry. (b) The all-zeros block is the operator B with matrix entries B_{ij} = <0^m,i|U|0^m,j>; the full set of equalities B_{ij} = A_{ij} for all i, j is literally the statement B = A as operators, so for EXACT embedding entrywise and operator identity coincide. For APPROXIMATE embedding, however, the definition controls the OPERATOR NORM of the difference, ||A - alpha B|| <= epsilon, not the individual entry errors. Operator norm is not controlled by entrywise size: a d-by-d matrix with every entry equal to a small delta has operator norm up to d*delta (e.g. the all-ones matrix times delta has norm d*delta), which grows with dimension even as each entry error delta stays tiny. Hence many small entry errors can accumulate coherently into a large operator-norm error, so entrywise closeness is neither the quantity the definition uses nor a sufficient accuracy guarantee; the correct certificate is a bound on the spectral/operator norm of A - alpha B.

question: A quantum computer natively applies only unitary operations, yet many scientific-computing tasks require applying a non-unitary matrix A. Show that this mismatch can always be bridged by dilation: given any n-qubit matrix A with operator norm at most 1 and singular value decomposition A = W Sigma V-dagger (W, V unitary, Sigma diagonal with entries in [0,1]), prove that the (n+1)-qubit operator built blockwise from W, V, Sigma and sqrt(I - Sigma^2), namely the product of diag(W, I), the 2x2-block matrix [[Sigma, sqrt(I-Sigma^2)],[sqrt(I-Sigma^2), -Sigma]], and diag(V-dagger, I), is unitary and has A exactly as its top-left block. Then explain why this does NOT mean A itself can be substituted by a single native unitary acting on the system register alone, i.e. why the extra ancilla and postselection are unavoidable when A is non-unitary.
reference_answer: Unitarity: the outer factors diag(W, I) and diag(V-dagger, I) are unitary because W, V are. For the middle factor M = [[Sigma, S],[S, -Sigma]] with S = sqrt(I - Sigma^2) (so S is diagonal, real, and S^2 = I - Sigma^2, and Sigma, S commute), compute M-dagger M. Since Sigma, S are real diagonal (hence Hermitian and mutually commuting), the (1,1) block is Sigma^2 + S^2 = Sigma^2 + (I - Sigma^2) = I; the (2,2) block is S^2 + Sigma^2 = I; the (1,2) block is Sigma S - S Sigma = 0 and the (2,1) block is S Sigma - Sigma S = 0. So M-dagger M = I and M is unitary. A product of unitaries is unitary, so the whole operator is unitary. Top-left block: multiplying out, the (1,1) block is W * Sigma * V-dagger = A (the other contributions to the (1,1) block vanish because the off-diagonal pieces of the outer factors are zero). Hence A is exactly the all-zeros-ancilla block, i.e. a unit-factor one-ancilla embedding of A. Why no direct unitary substitution: a native system-only unitary U_sys would satisfy U_sys-dagger U_sys = I, i.e. preserve all norms and be invertible with unitary inverse. A non-unitary A (for instance any A with a singular value strictly less than 1, or a singular/non-normal A) does not preserve norms and cannot equal any unitary, so no system-only native gate implements A. The dilation realizes A only as a block of a larger unitary; recovering A|b> requires preparing the ancilla, running the big unitary, and postselecting the all-zeros outcome (which succeeds with probability ||A|b>||^2 <= 1). The ancilla and the probabilistic postselection are exactly what absorb the non-unitarity (the shrinking of norms), so they are unavoidable whenever A is not itself unitary.

question: A target operator is written as a linear combination T = sum_i alpha_i U_i of unitaries U_i, and is implemented by a prepare-select-unprepare scheme in which each coefficient is split as alpha_i = beta_i gamma_i, a left preparation loads the vector of beta_i (normalized by the 2-norm of beta), a controlled selection applies U_i, and a right unpreparation loads the vector of gamma_i. The resulting construction embeds T with subnormalization factor equal to the product of the 2-norms of the beta and gamma vectors. Prove, using the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, that this subnormalization factor is at least the 1-norm of the coefficient vector alpha, and determine the splitting beta_i, gamma_i that makes the factor equal to that 1-norm. Explain why this is the best (smallest) achievable factor for this scheme and hence the most favorable success probability.
reference_answer: The scheme produces subnormalization factor ||beta||_2 ||gamma||_2 where ||beta||_2 = sqrt(sum_i |beta_i|^2) and likewise for gamma. Since alpha_i = beta_i gamma_i, the 1-norm of alpha is ||alpha||_1 = sum_i |alpha_i| = sum_i |beta_i| |gamma_i|. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality applied to the vectors (|beta_i|)_i and (|gamma_i|)_i, sum_i |beta_i| |gamma_i| <= sqrt(sum_i |beta_i|^2) sqrt(sum_i |gamma_i|^2) = ||beta||_2 ||gamma||_2. Therefore ||alpha||_1 <= ||beta||_2 ||gamma||_2, i.e. the subnormalization factor is at least ||alpha||_1 for every admissible split. Equality in Cauchy-Schwarz holds iff the vectors (|beta_i|) and (|gamma_i|) are proportional; combined with |beta_i gamma_i| = |alpha_i|, the symmetric optimum is |beta_i| = |gamma_i| = sqrt(|alpha_i|) for every i. With that choice ||beta||_2^2 = ||gamma||_2^2 = sum_i |alpha_i| = ||alpha||_1, so ||beta||_2 ||gamma||_2 = ||alpha||_1, attaining the lower bound. Since the success probability of keeping the all-zeros ancilla scales inversely with the square of the subnormalization factor, minimizing it to ||alpha||_1 maximizes the success probability for this prepare-select-unprepare implementation; no split in this scheme can do better, because ||alpha||_1 is a hard lower bound from Cauchy-Schwarz. (When all alpha_i >= 0 this optimal choice also makes the unpreparation the adjoint of the preparation.)
